title: The invoice tool that barely pays
scenario:
You are a finance analyst at a retail company. A vendor offers an AI tool that suggests accounting codes for supplier invoices. The vendor says it saves 4 minutes per invoice, so the team of clerks would save a lot of money.

You ran a pilot on 300 invoices and built an ROI model. The exhibit shows the inputs. The CFO asks you four things: the real monthly benefit, the payback time, which change would help most, and whether a cheaper plan is better.
exhibit:
Invoice coding pilot (made-up example data)

Invoices per month: 6,000
Clerk cost (loaded): $36 per hour = $0.60 per minute
Saved clerk time goes to the invoice backlog, which now needs overtime.

Result of the 300-invoice test
  Code is right: 88%. A clerk saves 4 minutes = $2.40
  Code is wrong: 12%
    90% of wrong codes are caught in review. Fixing costs
    $6.00 more than coding by hand.
    10% of wrong codes slip through. Fixing them later costs $80.

Per 1,000 invoices: 880 right (+$2,112),
  108 caught (-$648), 12 slipped (-$960) = +$504

Current plan: $2,500 licence + $400 usage per month
One-off set-up: $9,000

Cheaper plan: $2,300 per month in total.
  Accuracy on the same 300 invoices: 84%.
  Same shares of caught and slipped errors.

questions.prompt: What is the net benefit per month on the current plan?

options.explanation: This is the benefit from 6,000 invoices after errors, but before the $2,900 running cost is taken off.
This is the vendor's claim: 6,000 invoices × 4 minutes × $0.60. It counts no errors and no costs.
Right. With errors counted, the benefit is 6 × $504 = $3,024. Take off the $2,900 running cost, and $124 is left.
This counts only the invoices coded right (6 × $2,112 = $12,672) minus the $2,900 running cost. It ignores the cost of wrong codes.

questions.prompt: With a $9,000 one-off set-up, how long is the payback?

options.explanation: This uses the vendor's $14,400 claim. After the $2,900 running cost, about $11,500 would be left, but that figure ignores errors.
This divides $9,000 by $3,024 and forgets the $2,900 running cost.
Right. $9,000 ÷ $124 is about 73 months. The pilot pays back, but very slowly.
The net benefit is small, but it is positive: about $124 a month.

questions.prompt: Which change would raise the net benefit most?

options.explanation: This adds only about $250 a month.

options.text: Catch every wrong code in review.
options.explanation: Right. The 12 slipped errors per 1,000 invoices cost $960. Catching them costs $72 in fixes, so the gain is $888 per 1,000, about $5,300 a month.
This adds about $158 per 1,000 invoices, about $950 a month.

options.text: Save one more minute per right code.
options.explanation: This adds $0.60 on 880 invoices per 1,000, about $3,170 a month. It helps, but less than catching errors.

questions.prompt: The cheaper plan costs $2,300 a month and is 84% accurate. What follows?

options.text: Take it: running cost is $600 lower, so the net is higher.
options.explanation: The saving is real, but the extra errors cost more. At 84% the errors cost far more than $600 a month.

options.text: Skip it: at 84% accuracy the tool loses money every month.
options.explanation: Right. At 84%, 1,000 invoices give a net of about −$128 before running cost. That is about −$770 a month, and −$3,070 after the $2,300.

options.text: Take it: accuracy fell only four points, so the change is small.
options.explanation: Four points looks small, but each wrong code costs more than a right one earns.

options.text: Skip it: a cheaper plan is always worse than the current one.
options.explanation: Not always. The OpenAI docs say to keep the lightest setting that meets your quality bar. Here this one misses it.
